name: Zoe Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead operator on B shift at Kestrel Plastics, in the injection moulding hall. We make car parts, mostly air vent housings and the little clips that hold the door trim on. I've got eight presses in my cell, and my day is walking that line, listening to them, checking the first parts off every mould change and keeping the younger ones from cutting corners. I've been there sixteen years, and I'm also the union steward for my shift, which mostly means people find me in the canteen with their problems.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when a new mould goes in and I get it running clean before the setter even finishes his tea. You can hear a good press, honestly, it has a rhythm. What wears me out is the heat in summer and the pressure from upstairs, because every week there's a new number on the board we're supposed to hit. And the tablets they gave us for logging scrap, I'll be honest, I write it on paper and Agnes from quality types it in for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype? That I can believe. Every few years there's a new thing that's going to change the factory, and then it's the same presses and the same overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, probably in the canteen with a bit too much pleasure. Half the office has been going on about AI like it's the second coming. I'd say good, now maybe they'll spend the money on fixing the cooling on press six instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief. My worry was never the chatbot, it was the robot arms, and those were coming anyway, AI or not. So in this picture my life stays the same, which isn't perfect, but I know how to handle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep paying down the mortgage on Mill Lane and keep about three months put aside like we do now. I'd keep pushing the company on the next pay deal, same as every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, I suppose. A bit smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robot arms were coming anyway. What do you mean by that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We already have sprue pickers on four of my presses, little arms that pull the part out and drop it on the belt. When they came in, two operator posts went on nights and nobody said the word redundancy, they just didn't replace people who left. So I don't need AI to tell me the machines are coming, I've watched it happen one press at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas that night, if the news said AI was mostly hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He drives the number 14 bus, so he'd be more relieved than me, he's been reading about driverless buses. I'd say, see, we can stop checking the news every night and look at the holiday brochure. Then I'd probably still worry about the arms, because that's who I am.

S0.say: She'd say she told everyone so, with a bit too much pleasure, and that the company should spend the money on fixing the press cooling instead of on AI.
S0.think: It would be a relief, because her real worry is the robot arms, which were coming anyway. Her life stays the same, and she knows how to handle that.
S0.do: Keeps paying down the mortgage on Mill Lane and keeps about three months of savings aside as now. Carries on pushing the company in the yearly pay deal as union steward.
S0.quote: I don't need AI to tell me the machines are coming, I've watched it happen one press at a time.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe separates AI from robots in her head: the chatbot never scared her, the sprue pickers did. She already has a story of jobs lost by quiet non-replacement, and that story colours everything after this. Even in the calmest picture she says she'd still worry, and she owns that it's her nature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds less like a picture and more like what's already happening at our place, just faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union stronger, not weaker. If the company is saving money with new machines, some of that should come back to the people on the floor. I'd post that, and I'd say it at the branch meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my cell goes from eight operators to four inside three years. I'd probably keep my job, because they need someone who knows the moulds, but I'd be watching the others go. And I'm not someone who picks up new systems fast, so if they want me on screens all day, that's a real problem for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the branch and push for a no-compulsory-redundancy agreement before the new machines arrive, not after. At home we'd stop putting extra on the mortgage and build the savings from three months towards five. I'd keep doing my job as well as I can and let them see they need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not sleepless, but it's there all the time, like a press that's running a bit hot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kasia, who's been on my line two years. She's quick, but she's on a temporary contract, and the temps always go first. And Dariusz, the setter, who's 59 and swears he'll never touch a computer. He's even worse than me, and I'm bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not quick with new systems. Would you learn the screens if it meant keeping your post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, wouldn't I. But I'd want it taught properly, on paid time, by a person and not by a video on the tablet. That's what I'd fight for, because I know I'd struggle and I don't want to be made to feel stupid in front of my own line.

S1.say: She'd say this is why the union needs to be stronger, and that savings from new machines should come back to the people on the floor. She'd post it and raise it at the branch.
S1.think: Privately she thinks her cell shrinks from eight operators to four in three years. She'd likely keep her post because of her mould knowledge, but she isn't quick with new systems and that worries her.
S1.do: Pushes the union branch for a no-compulsory-redundancy deal before the new machines arrive. Stops overpaying the mortgage to grow savings from three months towards five, and keeps working hard so the company sees they need her.
S1.feel: Anxious, a steady background worry that's always there.
S1.quote: I'd want it taught properly, on paid time, by a person and not by a video on the tablet.
S1.fieldNote: Her first move is collective, not personal: she goes to the branch before she goes to her own savings. She's honest that her own resistance to screens is a weakness, and she wants training on terms that protect her dignity. Her worry reaches out to Kasia on a temporary contract and to Dariusz, who is even less ready than she is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Two years is nothing. Mila will be fifteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say the government has to step in, now, and stop companies firing whole factories overnight. I'd be at whatever protest the union called. I'd say this wasn't decided by anyone I voted for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be finished at Kestrel. If a robot can set a mould and judge a part by eye better than me, there's nothing left that's mine. I've got sixteen years of knowing those presses and it's worth nothing overnight. And I don't know what I'd do instead, I really don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd cancel the holiday and the new kitchen we've been saving towards. I'd ring the bank about a mortgage holiday before anyone else does. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd write to our MP, for what that's worth. If I got laid off I'd sign on straight away and probably look for cleaning or care work, something a robot isn't doing yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic. My chest goes tight just saying it. I feel like I'd have no time to even think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mila and Petr?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're going to be fine, because that's what you say. Then I'd go and sit in the car on the drive so they can't hear me. Petr's nine, he'd just ask if we can still get a dog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years of warning, is there anything you'd do differently in those two years than with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years there's no time to retrain, not for someone like me who takes a year to get used to a new tablet. So the two years would just be saving every penny and fighting. With more time I might actually try to learn something, but two years, I'd just be holding on.

S2.say: She'd say the government must step in now to stop companies emptying factories overnight, join any protest the union calls, and point out nobody voted for this.
S2.think: Privately she thinks she'd be finished at Kestrel, with sixteen years of press knowledge worth nothing overnight. She has no idea what she'd do instead.
S2.do: Cancels the holiday and the planned kitchen and asks the bank about a mortgage holiday early. Goes to every union meeting and writes to her MP, and if laid off claims benefits straight away and looks for cleaning or care work.
S2.feel: Panic, with a tight chest and no time to think.
S2.quote: With two years there's no time to retrain, not for someone like me who takes a year to get used to a new tablet.
S2.fieldNote: Two years removes the one thing Zoe relies on, which is time to fight and time to adjust slowly. She'd protect the kids from it and then cry in the car, which shows how much is held in. Her fallback ideas, care and cleaning, are about finding work robots haven't reached yet rather than work she wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's still fast, but it's at least a bit of runway. The mortgage still wouldn't be paid off, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to get the rules right, so let's not waste them arguing. Tax the companies that put in the robots and use it to keep people's wages going while they retrain. I'd be saying that at work and at the branch every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still lose the job, just later. But five years means Mila is done with school and maybe Tomas finds something steady. It means I could pay the mortgage down a bit more and not be quite so exposed when it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything spare onto the mortgage and the savings for the first three years. I'd get the union to push for retraining money now, not once we're out the door. And I'd probably make myself do one course, maybe the forklift and warehouse ticket, because warehouses might hold on a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd sleep, mostly, but I'd wake up at four some nights doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would worry you most in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, always. We've got eleven years left on it, and if the rate goes up while I'm on half pay, that's the house. Everything else, the car, the phone, the kids' football, we can cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you don't trust new systems. Would you really do a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I knew for sure it was coming, yes, I'd make myself. I wouldn't enjoy it and I'd probably moan the whole way through. But five years is enough that my stubbornness would cost my kids, and I won't let it.

S3.say: She'd say there are five years to get the rules right: tax companies that bring in robots and use it to keep wages going during retraining.
S3.think: She'd still lose her job, only later, but five years lets Mila finish school, gives Tomas time to find something steady, and lets them cut the mortgage down.
S3.do: Puts every spare bit onto the mortgage and savings for three years. Pushes the union for retraining money now and makes herself do one course, maybe a forklift and warehouse ticket.
S3.feel: Alarmed: mostly sleeping, but waking at four some nights doing sums.
S3.quote: Five years is enough that my stubbornness would cost my kids, and I won't let it.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turn Zoe from holding on to planning, but only just. She sees her own resistance clearly and decides, for the kids' sake, to push through it. The mortgage, with eleven years left, is the fixed point of all her fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be fifty-three. That's a different story, but the same ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time to do this decently if anyone wants to. Shorter hours, the same pay, a share of what the robots earn. I'd be saying that loudly, because ten years is also enough time for everyone to forget about it until it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd make it to fifty-something at Kestrel and then be pushed out. With ten years the mortgage would be nearly done and the kids would be grown. So it's not the end of the world for me, but I'd be furious for Kasia and the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to get a proper plan through the union, with a jobs guarantee or a decent payout for long service. I'd keep saving steadily, maybe get to six months. I'd stay where I am and keep my head down, because I'm not someone who jumps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but more angry than scared. I'd feel like I had time to fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between five years and ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten I don't have to change who I am. I can finish where I am, more or less, and the fight is about doing it properly for everybody else. With five I have to change, and I'm not good at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kasia, if she asked your advice with ten years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to get out of moulding and learn to fix the robots, or train for something with people in it. She's twenty-four, she's quick. I'd hate saying it, because it feels like giving up the trade, but it'd be the right advice.

S4.say: She'd say a decade is enough to do this decently, with shorter hours, the same pay and a share of what robots earn, and she'd say it loudly so people don't forget until it's too late.
S4.think: She'd probably last into her fifties at Kestrel before being pushed out, with the mortgage nearly done and the kids grown. She'd be furious for the younger workers more than for herself.
S4.do: Uses the first year to push a plan through the union, with a jobs guarantee or a decent long-service payout. Keeps saving steadily towards six months and stays in her job.
S4.feel: Still anxious, but more angry than scared, with a sense of time to fight.
S4.quote: With ten I don't have to change who I am.
S4.fieldNote: For Zoe, ten years means she can avoid changing herself, which is what she fears most. Her energy shifts from her own family to the younger workers, and she'd tell Kasia to leave the trade even though it hurts to say. The gap between five and ten years is, for her, the gap between having to adapt and being allowed not to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is something in writing before it happens, a law that says if you put in robots you keep paying people for a set time while they retrain. And help with the mortgage, a pause that doesn't wreck your credit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money. Everyone asks what we'll do, nobody asks where the savings go. If the presses run themselves, somebody's getting richer, and it won't be anyone on B shift. I've spent sixteen years making other people's car parts and I'd like a straight answer on that.

headlineQuote: If the presses run themselves, somebody's getting richer, and it won't be anyone on B shift.
portrait: Zoe Novak is 43, the lead operator on B shift in the injection moulding hall at Kestrel Plastics and the union steward for her shift. She has watched robot arms quietly replace operator posts already, so she sees robots, not chatbots, as the real threat. She avoids new technology and admits it, still logging scrap on paper. She moves from calm in the hype picture to panic when AGI arrives in two years, because she has no time to adapt, while ten years would let her finish her career and fight for younger workers instead. Her answers keep coming back to the union, the mortgage on Mill Lane and who gets the savings.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries her most, because there's no time for someone slow with new systems to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring companies that bring in robots to keep paying workers for a set time while they retrain, and a mortgage pause that doesn't damage her credit.
